title: Traffic Estimation & QPS
summary: Turning DAU/MAU into queries-per-second, and why the read/write ratio, the peak multiplier, and fan-out all change what number you actually design for.

slides.markdown:
Every capacity conversation starts from **queries per second** — how many requests a second the system must serve. You never get QPS directly; you derive it from a user count and a per-user action rate, then correct for two things people forget: traffic isn't flat over a day, and one user action can trigger many backend requests.

This topic builds that derivation step by step: DAU to requests, requests to average QPS, average to peak QPS, and peak to the *effective* QPS after fan-out.

slides.sectionTitle: From DAU/MAU to requests per second
slides.markdown:
**DAU** (daily active users) is your starting point; if you're only given **MAU** (monthly active users), apply a stickiness ratio — a daily-habit app might see 20% of MAU active on a given day, so 250 million MAU implies roughly 50 million DAU (250,000,000 × 0.20).

From there: multiply DAU by requests-per-user-per-day, then divide by seconds-in-a-day. 50 million DAU × 20 requests/user/day = 1 billion requests/day. Divide by ~86,400 seconds (or the rounded 10^5 shortcut) and you land around 10,000-12,000 requests per second, on average.

That average is a starting point, not the number you design for — the next slides correct it.

slides.sectionTitle: Read-heavy vs write-heavy: why the ratio changes your design
slides.markdown:
Two systems with identical total QPS can need completely different architectures, because *what kind* of traffic dominates changes the bottleneck. A consumer feed is typically **read-heavy** — users scroll far more than they post, and ratios of 100 reads to 1 write are common. A logging or metrics pipeline is the opposite: **write-heavy**, close to all ingest, almost no reads until someone runs a query.

Read-heavy systems lean on caching and read replicas, since the same data gets fetched over and over. Write-heavy systems lean on append-friendly storage (write-optimized log-structured stores) and batching, since the write path is what saturates first.

Name the dominant direction before you design — it decides where you spend your engineering effort.

slides.sectionTitle: Average QPS vs peak QPS: the multiplier you must not skip
slides.markdown:
Average QPS describes a full day smoothed flat — it is never the number that takes a system down. Outages happen at **peak**: the evening rush, lunchtime, a viral post. A typical consumer app sees a peak-to-average ratio of roughly **2-3x** on an ordinary day, and 10x or more during a spike like a flash sale or breaking news.

If your average is 10,000 QPS and you provision for exactly 10,000, the system is overloaded for every hour above average — which, on a normal diurnal curve, is about half the day.

Always multiply: provision for peak QPS (average × peak-to-average ratio), then add headroom on top of that for growth and safety margin.

slides.sectionTitle: Diagram: traffic curve over a day and the peak-to-average ratio
slides.markdown:
![24-hour traffic curve with a trough near 3-5am and a broad evening peak roughly 2.5-3x the flat average line, with the gap labelled peak-to-average ratio](assets/daily-traffic-curve.svg)

Real traffic isn't flat — it tracks when people are awake, with a trough overnight and a peak in the evening. The average line on this chart is the number your back-of-envelope math produces; the peak is the number that actually determines whether the system falls over.

The gap between those two lines is exactly the multiplier from the previous slide — read it off a real traffic graph when you have one, and assume 2-3x when you don't.

slides.sectionTitle: Worked example: estimating QPS for a social feed, step by step
slides.markdown:
Assumptions: 10 million DAU, each opens the feed 8 times/day (1 read request per open), and 1 in 10 users posts once a day.

```
Reads/day  = 10,000,000 users x 8 opens        = 80,000,000
Writes/day = 10,000,000 users x 0.1 posts      =  1,000,000

Avg read QPS  = 80,000,000 / 86,400 s  ≈  926 QPS
Avg write QPS =  1,000,000 / 86,400 s  ≈   12 QPS

Read:write ratio ≈ 926 : 12 ≈ 80:1   (confirms read-heavy)

Apply a 3x peak multiplier:
Peak read QPS  ≈ 926 x 3  ≈ 2,780 QPS
Peak write QPS ≈  12 x 3  ≈    35 QPS
```

Notice the ratio (80:1) falls out of the per-user action rates, not an assumption you had to guess — that's the check that your inputs were reasonable.

slides.sectionTitle: Compare: estimating QPS for a read-heavy feed vs a write-heavy logging system
slides.markdown:
The estimation steps are the same; the numbers that matter flip.

| | Read-heavy feed | Write-heavy logging |
|---|---|---|
| Typical read:write | ~100:1 or higher | close to all writes, reads are rare/batch |
| Dominant bottleneck | cache hit rate, read replica capacity | write throughput, ingest buffering |
| What to size for | peak read QPS + cache miss rate | peak write QPS + burst tolerance |
| Common fix | caching layer, read replicas | log-structured storage, batching writes |

**How to decide:** ask what the user's most frequent action is — viewing (read-heavy) or generating events (write-heavy) — and size the tier that action hits hardest, not both tiers equally.

slides.sectionTitle: Pitfall: forgetting fan-out multiplies effective QPS
slides.markdown:
**Wrong belief:** "I calculated 12 write QPS for new posts, so the system needs to handle 12 writes a second."

**Why it's wrong:** if each post fans out to update, say, 500 followers' timelines (a push model), every logical write becomes 500 physical writes downstream. The timeline-write path actually sees roughly 12 × 500 ≈ 6,000 writes a second — nearly 500x the naive figure.

**Correct model:** identify every fan-out point in the request path — one write triggering many writes, or one read triggering many backend calls — and multiply before sizing that tier. The QPS you calculated from user actions is only the starting point of the chain, not the end of it.
